_comment: Hindu expansion 175-drive B: Rigveda story-hymns (marriage, twins, dawn-maidens, gambling, sacrifice). Griffith 1896, public domain.

title.en: The Bridal of Surya, the Sun's Daughter

region.zh: 旁遮普平原（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Rigveda, Book 10, Hymn 85, c. 1200-1000 BCE (Griffith translation, 1896)

source.work: The Hymns of the Rigveda, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1896), Book 10, Hymn 85 (Surya's bridal)

summary.en: The most beautiful hymn of the Rigveda is a wedding: Surya, the Sun's daughter, is wooed over the sky-road by Soma, Gandharva, and Agni in turn, and weds Soma with all the gods as guests. The hymn is the charter of Vedic marriage itself - every Hindu wedding still recites its vows about the bride's sun-kissed, wide-prospering husband.
summary.zh: 梨俱吠陀最美的頌詩是一場婚禮：日女蘇利耶經天路先後受蘇摩、乾達婆與阿耆尼求聘，終嫁蘇摩，諸神皆為賓客。此頌即吠陀婚姻本身的憲章——至今印度婚禮仍誦其關於夫婿如日般廣受福澤的誓詞。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition: hymn recited at Hindu weddings; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: Truth was the beam of her bridal house, the rite its roof; the verses were the joining-car, and the songs its pillars - so the hymn builds Surya's house out of the sacrifice itself before her grooms arrive.

Her suitors came over the high road of the sky: first Soma the moon won her, then Gandharva claimed her, then Agni held her - and to Soma, the gods gave the sun-maiden perfected: the wedding-gifts went round, the guests assembled.

The vows are domestic and cosmic at once: pure, I give thee the husband of a wide and sun-shining dominion; may he prosper in thy keeping; and the crowd of the gods' people, the Anumatis, came to watch the daughter of the Sun carried in procession.

The marriage of Surya became the marriage of every bride: the bridegroom's friends, the chariot, the veil, the swinging of the bride's foot over the threshold - the hymn invents in ritual what it names in myth.

title.zh: 雙馬童使老仙人契耶凡納返老還童

region.zh: 旁遮普平原（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Rigveda, Book 1, Hymns 116-117, c. 1500-1200 BCE (Griffith translation, 1896)

source.work: The Hymns of the Rigveda, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1896), Book 1, Hymns 116-117 (the Ashvins' deeds)

summary.en: The Ashvins, divine twin horsemen and physicians of the gods, renewed the aged sage Chyavana: they stripped the skin of his decrepitude from him as it were a garment, gave him a new body, and - in the Brahmana's telling - were rewarded with Soma, the only drink Indra denied them. Doctors of dawn and dusk, they save the drowning and mend the broken.
summary.zh: 雙馬童，諸神的騎手神醫，使年邁的仙人契耶凡納返老還童：他們如剝衣般剝下其老朽之皮，賜以新身——梵書言其因此獲得蘇摩，那是因陀羅唯一拒予雙神之飲。晨昏二位的醫者，既救溺水者，也修補折損者。

passages.text: The two young heroes, the Nasatyas, ride the earliest car over sea and sky, thundering with their horses at daybreak and at dusk - healers who come at the hour between night and day, when no other god will answer.

For Chyavana, grown old among his sons like a spent king, they stripped the withered skin from his body and wrapped him in new: the old man came out of his decrepitude with the beauty of youth restored.

In the Brahmana's longer telling the twins' fee for the renewal was a draught of Soma, which Indra forbade to them; Chyavana, insulted, barred the door against Indra - and the god of a thousand eyes could not enter until the physicians of the gods had shared the cup.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Ashvins-Chyavana story (Brahmana tradition; Griffith 1896 hymns); not verbatim.

title.zh: 薩羅摩追蹤被竊的牛群

texts.period: Rigveda, Book 10, Hymn 108, c. 1200-1000 BCE (Griffith translation, 1896)

source.work: The Hymns of the Rigveda, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1896), Book 10, Hymn 108 (Sarama and the Panis)

summary.en: The Panis - the grasping merchant-demons - stole the cows of light into a rock cave. The divine hound Sarama, Indra's messenger, tracks them across the nine-and-ninety rivers and stands at the cave mouth; the Panis try to bribe her; she refuses, and her word for Indra is the war-cry that opens the rock.
summary.zh: 潘尼——貪婪的商魔——把光之牛群偷進岩洞。神犬薩羅摩，因陀羅的信使，跨九十九河追蹤，立於洞口；潘尼試圖賄賂她；她拒絕，其向因陀羅的回話即裂岩開洞的戰呼。

passages.text: The Panis drove the kine of light into the hollow of the rock and hid them: their city of the stolen goods lies beyond the nine-and-ninety rivers, past which only the nose of the divine hound could follow.

Sarama, sent as Indra's spy, found them and stood at the cave's mouth; the Panis offered her partnership - a share of the stolen herds if she would sell her lord's plan. She answered as a messenger must: I come to see your fortress, and my word is Indra's.

Her report is the hymn's engine: let the Panis know their cattle will be carried back by force; and when Indra and the Angiras seers split the rock, the cows of the dawns lowed out of the cave to their old pastures - light ransacked back from the hoarders.

title.en: The Cave of Vala: Dawn Rescued from the Rock
title.zh: 伐羅之洞：自岩中救回的黎明

source.work: The Hymns of the Rigveda, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1896), Book 10, Hymn 72 and hymns to Vala (e.g. 2.12, 1.62)

summary.en: Vala, a demon split from his own father's sacrifice, swallowed the dawns and the cows of light and sat on them inside stone. The Angiras seers - the poets themselves as priests of dawn - climbed the rock, sang the stone open, and Vala burst; the Ushases, the goddesses of dawn, lowed out like cows to the pastures of the sky.
summary.zh: 伐羅，自其父祭中裂出的惡魔，吞下黎明與光之牛，端坐於石內。盎耆羅仙人——詩人自己作為黎明的祭司——攀上岩石，以歌裂石，伐羅爆裂；烏莎斯諸女，黎明女神們，如母牛般哞叫著走向天上的牧野。

passages.text: From the sacrifice of the gods Vala was split off, the first-born of seizure: he swallowed the cows and the dawns, and sat over them in the heart of stone - a hoard of light locked under rock.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda hymns to Vala (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Angiras, the chanters of old, set their song against the stone: they climbed it as men climb a ladder, and with their hymns carved like axes they cracked the mountain; the rocks opened like a split melon.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda hymns to Vala (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: Out of the cave came the Ushases lowing like kine at milking-time, finding their pastures of the sky again; the metaphor is the theology - dawn is cattle, and the poet's voice is the herdsman's tool.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda hymns to Vala (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.

title.en: Svarbhanu Pierces the Sun with Darkness
title.zh: 斯伐爾巴努以黑暗貫穿太陽

region.zh: 旁遮普平原（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Rigveda, Book 5, Hymn 40, c. 1500-1200 BCE (Griffith translation, 1896)

source.work: The Hymns of the Rigveda, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1896), Book 5, Hymn 40 (the darkening of the Sun)

summary.en: The Asura Svarbhanu, the sun-swallower, pierced the Sun with darkness so that the sky itself could not see; the world went blind at midday. Indra struck down the demon, but the Sun's sight was broken - and the blind god was led, like a patient, to the Ashvins, the twin physicians, who restored his eye: the Vedas' own eclipse myth and its cure.
summary.zh: 阿修羅斯伐爾巴努，吞日者，以黑暗貫穿太陽，使天穹亦不能視；正午的世界陷入盲暗。因陀羅擊落惡魔，但日神之目已損——盲眼之神如病者被引至雙馬童，二位神醫復其目：吠陀自有的蝕神話與其療法。

passages.text: O Surya, when the Asura's son Svarbhanu pierced thee through with darkness, all creatures looked like men bewildered who know not where they stand.
Indra alone pierced the monster with his bolt; Atri, the sage, set the Sun upon the sky's road again - but the god's eye was hurt, and the night of midday did not lift.

Then Atri took the blind Sun and led him to the two Ashvins as one leads a suffering king: they restored his sight with their remedies, and the hymn closes on the freed light - the eclipse explained, exorcised, and healed.

region.zh: 旁遮普平原（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Rigveda, Book 10, Hymn 34, c. 1200-1000 BCE (Griffith translation, 1896)

source.work: The Hymns of the Rigveda, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1896), Book 10, Hymn 34 (the dice)

summary.en: The Rigveda's most personal poem is a confession of gambling ruin: the dice, 'born on a cold night with the magic herb', are praised as gods and blamed as demons; the speaker's wife hates him, his mother-in-law hunts him, and he ends homeless in the dark 'not knowing what I may get by the dice'. The oldest literature on addiction.
summary.zh: 梨俱吠陀最私人的一首詩是賭徒破產的自白：骰子『生於寒夜、與魔草相伴』，被譽為神又被斥為魔；說話者被妻所憎、被岳母所逐，最後『不知擲骰能得何物』地流落黑暗。關於成癮的最古老文獻。

passages.text: The dice sprang high and rattled on the board; born on a cold night with the magic herb, they give delight and take a man's house: the gambler goes to the assembly hot from the hand, and never asks what fortune may do to him.
The confession: my wife despised me for the dice, my mother-in-law even worse; no one lends to a gambler, and like an old horse worn out under the saddle I dwell in another man's house in the dark.

The vow at the end is the first written self-reform: I will not play with them again; leave the men to their winnings, let me be - and the hymn ends with the dice's own fair warning: they have no pity even for the man who knows better.

title.en: Shunahshepa: The Boy Bound to the Post
title.zh: 設首施加：縛於祭柱的男孩

region.zh: 伐樓那之境（象徵性定位於布施伽爾）

texts.period: Rigveda, Book 5, Hymns 2-3 (his own hymns); Aitareya Brahmana tradition (Griffith translation, 1896)

source.work: The Hymns of the Rigveda, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1896), Book 5, Hymns 2-3 (hymns attributed to Shunahshepa), with the Brahmana narrative

summary.en: King Harishchandra, childless, vowed to Varuna that his first son would be sacrificed. The boy Rohita escaped into the wilds for years; at last he bought a poor man's son, Shunahshepa, to be tied to the post in his place. Bound before the fire, the boy sang to Varuna - and the god released him: he was adopted by the seer Vishvamitra and became a singer of hymns. The myth behind 'substitutionary sacrifice'.
summary.zh: 王哈利什陀羅無子，向伐樓那起誓以其首子獻祭。男孩羅希塔遁入荒野多年；終以貧者之子的兒子設首施加代替自己縛上祭柱。男孩縛於火前，向伐樓那唱頌——神遂釋之：他被維什瓦米陀收養，成為頌歌歌手。『替代祭』背後的神話。

passages.text: Harishchandra had vowed his son to Varuna for a son's sake; Rohita, grown, refused the stake and fled to the wilderness; the king was swollen with dropsy as long as the debt stood unpaid.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Shunahshepa story (Brahmana tradition); not verbatim.

passages.text: In his wandering years the prince met Ajigarta the starving and bought his son Shunahshepa for a hundred kine - the father took the price and agreed to bind the boy; the boy agreed to go.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Shunahshepa story (Brahmana tradition); not verbatim.

passages.text: Bound at the sacrificial post, the knife ready, Shunahshepa prayed to the gods with the hymns that still bear his name; Varuna, hearing, released the victim and healed the king - and Vishvamitra adopted the boy as a son among his hundred, calling him 'the singer saved at the post'.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Shunahshepa story with Rigveda 5.2-3 (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.

title.en: Lopamudra and Agastya: The Wife's Reckoning
title.zh: 羅帕穆德拉與阿竭多：妻子之秤

region.zh: 阿竭多仙居，南方山地（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Rigveda, Book 1, Hymn 179, c. 1500-1200 BCE (Griffith translation, 1896)

source.work: The Hymns of the Rigveda, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1896), Book 1, Hymn 179 (dialogue of Agastya and Lopamudra)

summary.en: Agastya, the pot-born dwarf sage, married the princess Lopamudra - chosen because her beauty was equal to heaven's. She told him plainly that austerity could not replace a household: 'the man who knows the gods, teach me; I desire offspring as a bride desires her lord'. He practiced austerity until his efforts bore two sons - and the Rigveda preserves her part of the argument, one of the oldest poems in the world spoken by a woman.
summary.zh: 罐中所生的矮小仙人阿竭多娶了公主羅帕穆德拉——因其美貌堪比天界。她直告他：苦行不能替代家室：『知神者，教我；我求子嗣，如新娘求其主。』他力行苦行直至生出二子——梨俱吠陀保存了她那一半的辯論，世上最古老的由女性口出的詩篇之一。

passages.text: Agastya chose his bride with a strange standard: beauty that matched heaven; Lopamudra, framed by the gods and given to the king of Kashi, chose the ascetic's hut instead of the palace she left.

The wife's verses press the point with wit: the aged sage grows old in austerity while the bride is a bride; not austerity, but giving, is the way of the ancestors - the fathers praised the seer and called his manliness incomplete.

He answered with effort: the hymn counts his labors like an athlete's log - hundreds and thousands of recitations, hunger, thirst, heat - until by his exertion two sons were born, the first to milk and the second a singer; the couple's joint credit is recorded in the same breath.

region.zh: 旁遮普平原（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Rigveda, Book 7, Hymn 103, c. 1500-1200 BCE (Griffith translation, 1896)

source.work: The Hymns of the Rigveda, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1896), Book 7, Hymn 103 (the frogs)

summary.en: The Rigveda's comic masterpiece: the frogs of the dried pond wake when the rains come, 'one lows like a cow, one bleats like a goat, one is speckled' - and the hymn blesses them as Brahmins keeping vigil at the sacrifice of the year. Creation-by-monsoon, told with the priests' own jokes.
summary.zh: 梨俱吠陀的滑稽傑作：乾涸池塘的青蛙在雨至時醒來——『一者如母牛而哞，一者如山羊而咩，一者斑駁』——頌詩祝福牠們如守年度之祭的婆羅門。季風所造的世界，以祭司自己的笑話講述。

passages.text: At rest for a year like Brahmins keeping a vow of silence, the frogs cry out when Parjanya, the rain-god, has watered the land: the voice rises from the drying pond like the singing of boys at school.

They are catalogued with tenderness and fun: one lows like a cow, one bleats like a goat, one is speckled, one is green - and they come from out the waters to the pool, talking as their kind talk, laughing over the water's edge.

The blessing is real: twelve months of drought they keep, and men cannot tell the season they mark; then the rain-year comes - and the hymn gives the frogs their reward, wealth of cows in a new monsoon, wealth of the singing word.

title.en: The Widow at the Husband's Pyre

region.zh: 旁遮普平原（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Rigveda, Book 10, Hymn 18, c. 1200-1000 BCE (Griffith translation, 1896)

source.work: The Hymns of the Rigveda, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1896), Book 10, Hymn 18 (funeral hymn; verses on the widow)

summary.en: The funeral hymn contains the tradition's earliest word on widowhood: the mourners address the woman at her husband's pyre - 'rise up, woman, to the world of the living; you lie by one whose life is spent' - and take the bow from the dead man's hand, breaking it for the living heir. The verse is the charter later cited against suttee; and the debate about its last lines has not ended.
summary.zh: 葬歌含傳統關於寡婦最早之言：哀悼者向火堆旁的女子說——『起來，女子，去活人的世界；你枕著的是一位生命已盡者』——並自死者手中取弓，為在世的繼承人折斷之。此節即後世反對寡婦殉葬者所引之憲章；而其末節的爭論至今未止。

sensitivity.note: Ancient funeral hymn, politically and morally contested in modern readings (suttee debate); classified 'myth'. The interpretive dispute is recorded here.

passages.text: The hymn sends the dead man forward to the fathers with his body, his eye to the Sun, his breath to the Wind - and turns to the living: let not our mothers weep; let the household be spared.

To the widow the verse speaks with a hand on her shoulder: rise, come to the world of the living, woman; thou liest by this one whose life is gone - the husband taking thy hand was thy first duty; widowhood is the second.

From the dead man's hand the bow is taken - a strong token for us, the mourners say - and broken, that he may not harm our fathers and may not harm us; the verse's margins hold the long later argument about what the woman was then commanded to do.
